claim: A subset of atypical memory B cells accumulates in malaria and several infections, autoimmune disorders and aging in both humans and mice.
source: A subset of atypical memory B cells accumulates in malaria and several infections, autoimmune disorders and aging in both humans and mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to Knox et al., 2017b; Naradikian et al., 2016a; Portugal et al., 2017; Rubtsov et al., 2017 in the manuscript text.

claim: Atypical memory B cells have been suggested to be exhausted long-lived memory B cells.
source: It has been suggested these cells are exhausted long-lived memory B cells, and their accumulation may contribute to poor acquisition of long-lasting immunity to certain chronic infections, such as malaria and HIV.
evidence: This is a statement about what has been suggested in the literature, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Plasmodium-specific atypical memory B cells are short-lived.
source: Here, we generated an immunoglobulin heavy chain knock-in mouse with a BCR that recognizes MSP1 of the rodent malaria parasite, Plasmodium chabaudi. In combination with a mosquito-initiated P. chabaudi infection, we show that Plasmodium-specific atypical memory B cells are short-lived and disappear upon natural resolution of chronic infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the IghNIMP23/+ mouse model showing AMB disappear after infection resolution.

claim: Plasmodium-specific atypical memory B cells disappear upon natural resolution of chronic infection.
source: we show that Plasmodium-specific atypical memory B cells are short-lived and disappear upon natural resolution of chronic infection.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B cells are not detected above background at 155dpi.

claim: Plasmodium-specific atypical memory B cells show features of activation, proliferation, DNA replication, and plasmablasts.
source: These cells show features of activation, proliferation, DNA replication, and plasmablasts.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data showing expression of Mki67, cell cycle genes, and plasmablast markers.

claim: Plasmodium-specific atypical memory B cells are not a subset of long-lived memory B cells.
source: Our data demonstrate that Plasmodium-specific atypical memory B cells are not a subset of long-lived memory B cells, but rather short-lived activated cells, and part of a physiologic ongoing B-cell response.
evidence: Supported by data showing these cells disappear after infection resolution and have pro-apoptotic gene expression.

claim: Plasmodium-specific atypical memory B cells are short-lived activated cells and part of a physiologic ongoing B-cell response.
source: Our data demonstrate that Plasmodium-specific atypical memory B cells are not a subset of long-lived memory B cells, but rather short-lived activated cells, and part of a physiologic ongoing B-cell response.
evidence: Supported by data showing AMB are generated in response to immunization and disappear rapidly, and by their activated transcriptional profile.

claim: Atypical memory B cells were first described in HIV-viremic subjects.
source: In the context of infections, AMB were first described in HIV-viremic subjects, and termed tissue-like memory B cells, due to their similarity to an FCRL4-expressing memory B-cell subset found in human tonsillar tissues (Ehrhardt et al., 2005; Moir et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ehrhardt et al., 2005 and Moir et al., 2008.

claim: Human atypical memory B cells express FCRL4.
source: In addition to FCRL4, these cells express relatively high levels of other potentially inhibitory receptors including CD22, CD85j, CD85k, LAIR-1, CD72, and PD-1
evidence: Supported by citations in the introduction describing human AMB characteristics.

claim: Human atypical memory B cells express high levels of inhibitory receptors including CD22, CD85j, CD85k, LAIR-1, CD72, and PD-1.
source: In addition to FCRL4, these cells express relatively high levels of other potentially inhibitory receptors including CD22, CD85j, CD85k, LAIR-1, CD72, and PD-1
evidence: Supported by citations describing human AMB characteristics.

claim: Human atypical memory B cells express trafficking receptors including CD11b, CD11c and CXCR3.
source: and show a profile of trafficking receptors including expression of CD11b, CD11c and CXCR3, consistent with migration to inflamed tissues.
evidence: Supported by citations describing human AMB characteristics.

claim: Human atypical memory B cells are antigen-experienced class-switched B cells.
source: They are antigen-experienced class-switched B cells, which lack the expression of CD21 and the hallmark human memory B-cell marker CD27.
evidence: Supported by citations describing human AMB characteristics.

claim: Human atypical memory B cells lack expression of CD21 and CD27.
source: They are antigen-experienced class-switched B cells, which lack the expression of CD21 and the hallmark human memory B-cell marker CD27.
evidence: Supported by citations describing human AMB characteristics.

claim: Human atypical memory B cells express the transcription factor T-bet.
source: Further studies demonstrated the expression of the transcription factor T-bet and the cytokine IFNγ by these cells, also characteristic of Th1 CD4+ T cells (Knox et al., 2017b; Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Knox et al., 2017b; Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2017.

claim: Human atypical memory B cells express IFNγ.
source: Further studies demonstrated the expression of the transcription factor T-bet and the cytokine IFNγ by these cells, also characteristic of Th1 CD4+ T cells (Knox et al., 2017b; Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Knox et al., 2017b; Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017; Portugal et al., 2017.

claim: Atypical memory B cells show poor functional capacity upon in vitro re-stimulation with BCR ligands.
source: Due to their poor functional capacity upon in vitro re-stimulation with BCR ligands, AMB were characterized as dysfunctional B cells, and increased frequencies of these cells was proposed to be a consequence of B-cell exhaustion driven by chronic inflammation and stimulation, drawing parallels with T-cell exhaustion during chronic viral infections (Moir et al., 2008; Portugal et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moir et al., 2008; Portugal et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015.

claim: The IghNIMP23/+ mice had approximately 60% of B cells specific for MSP121.
source: Importantly, The IghNIMP23/+ mice had a greatly increased frequency of B cells specific for MSP121 (approximately 60% of the total B-cell compartment), as demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis of splenocytes with a MSP121 fluorescent probe consisting of biotinylated recombinant MSP121 loaded on streptavidin-PE (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Most endogenous light chains pair with the NIMP23 heavy chain to generate a BCR with detectable binding to MSP121.
source: Thus, in this model, a recombinant light chain is not required to bring about specificity. This suggest that most endogenous light chains will pair with the NIMP23 heavy chain to generate a BCR with detectable binding to MSP121.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that high frequency of MSP121-specific B cells are detected without introducing a specific light chain.

claim: NIMP23→Rag2-/- mice infected with P. chabaudi by mosquito bite showed a similar course of parasitemia to control WT→Rag2-/- mice.
source: NIMP23→Rag2-/- mice infected with P. chabaudi by mosquito bite, showed a similar course of parasitemia to that of control WT→Rag2-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), and C57BL/6J wt mice (Brugat et al., 2017; Spence et al., 2013; Spence et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by parasitemia data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and citations to previous studies.

claim: MSP121-specific B cells showed a robust response to P. chabaudi infection with increased germinal center and class-switched B cells at 35 days post-infection.
source: Importantly, the MSP121-specific IghNIMP23/+ B cells (CD45.2+MSP121+) in NIMP23→Rag2-/- chimeras showed a robust response to the infection, as demonstrated by a dramatic increase in the proportions and numbers of GL-7+CD38lo germinal centers (GC) and IgG2b+IgD— class-switched B cells in the spleen at 35 days post-infection (dpi) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G-H.

claim: A distinct CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B-cell subset was detected at 28-35dpi during chronic P. chabaudi infection.
source: We detected an increased number of cells in a distinct CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B-cell subset at 28-35dpi, in the chronic phase of P. chabaudi infection (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B-cell subset showed high expression of FCRL5 and low expression of CD21 and IgD.
source: This subset showed several AMB characteristics, including high expression of FCRL5 and low expression of CD21 and IgD (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: The CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B-cell subset was enriched with cells expressing CD80 and CD273.
source: In addition, the CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B-cell subset was enriched with cells expressing CD80 and CD273 (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B cells were not significantly detected above background level after resolution of infection (155dpi onwards).
source: Unexpectedly, the numbers of CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B cells were not significantly higher than background level (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A-B at 155dpi.

claim: CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B cells highly expressed mouse homologues of genes upregulated in human AMB including IgG, Cxcr3, Tbx21, Lair1 and Fcrl5.
source: A series of hallmark genes upregulated in human AMB were also upregulated in CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B cells, including IgG (Ighg2c and Ighg2b), Cxcr3, Tbx21 (T-bet), Lair1 and Fcrl5 (Figure 3, genes in red boxes, and references in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells showed upregulation of Ifng, Aicda, inhibitory receptors, antigen-experienced/memory markers, and class-switched immunoglobulins.
source: In addition, the MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B-cell subset showed upregulation of Ifng, Aicda, a large array of inhibitory receptors [including Pd1, Cd72, Cd85k, Fcgr2b (CD32b), Siglece], antigen-experienced/memory markers [Cd80, Cd86, Nt5e (CD73) and high Cd38], and additional class-switched immunoglobulins (i.e. Igha, Ighg1 and Ighg3), all of which have been shown to be upregulated on human AMB (Figure 3C–G, references in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3C-G.

claim: MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells expressed Galectins (Lgals1 and Lgals3).
source: These cells also expressed Galectins (Lgals1 and Lgals3), previously implicated in B-cell anergy (Clark et al., 2007) (Figure 3H)
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3H and citation to Clark et al., 2007.

claim: MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells displayed a pro-apoptotic program with high expression of Fasl and low expression of Bcl2.
source: and displayed a pro-apoptotic program (e.g. high expression of Fasl, and low expression of Bcl2) (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells showed upregulation of Mki67, indicative of proliferation.
source: Interestingly, in agreement with data on human AMB, MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells showed upregulation of Mki67 (Figure 3J), indicative of proliferation
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells had characteristics of plasmablasts and/or plasma cells, including upregulation of Cd138, Prdm1 and Xbp1, and low expression of Cxcr5, Pax5, and Bcl6.
source: and had characteristics of plasmablasts and/or plasma cells, including upregulation of Cd138, Prdm1 (Blimp1) and Xbp1, and low expression of Cxcr5, Pax5, and Bcl6 (Figure 3B and K).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3B and K.

claim: MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells showed low expression of Irf4 and S1p1, suggesting they may be in a pre-plasmablast or pre-migratory plasma-cell stage.
source: However, these cells showed low expression of Irf4 and S1p1, suggesting that they may be in a pre-plasmablast or pre-migratory plasma-cell stage (Kabashima et al., 2006; Kallies et al., 2007) (Figure 3K).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3K and citations to Kabashima et al., 2006 and Kallies et al., 2007.

claim: CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B cells showed low expression of Cd40, Cr2, Ms4a1, and Cd24a.
source: Finally, and similar to human AMB, CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B cells showed low expression of Cd40, Cr2 (CD21), Ms4a1 (CD20), and Cd24a (Figure 3L).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis showed MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ AMB were enriched for gene sets corresponding to cell cycle, DNA replication, energy generation/consumption, regulation of apoptosis, activation of NF-κB, and BCR signaling.
source: Among the gene sets yielding the top 50 significant (fdr <0.001) highest normalized enrichment score (NES) we obtained gene sets corresponding to cell cycle, DNA replication, generation/consumption of energy, regulation of apoptosis, activation of NF-κB on B cells, and downstream signaling events of the BCR (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Substantial numbers of MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells were observed in spleens of IghNIMP23/+ mice 24 hr post-immunization with R848 and MSP121.
source: We observed substantial numbers of MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells in the spleens of IghNIMP23/+ mice 24 hr post-immunization (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells generated after immunization expressed increased levels of FCRL5 and CD80.
source: These cells expressed increased levels of both FCRL5 and CD80 (Figure 4B–C)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells generated after immunization did not display germinal center characteristics.
source: and did not display GC characteristics (Figure 4D), similar to the MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+FCRL5+ atypical B cells generated following Plasmodium infection.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells observed after immunization appeared only transiently and could no longer be detected at 3 and 7 days post-immunization.
source: The MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ B cells observed after immunization appeared only transiently, as they could no longer be detected at 3 and 7d post-immunization (Figure 4A and E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A and E.

claim: CD80+CD273+, CD80+CD273— and CD80—CD273+ MSP121-specific B cells, both class-switched and non-class-switched, were detected above background levels at 28-35dpi in P. chabaudi-infected mice.
source: By contrast, CD80+CD273+, CD80+CD273— and CD80—CD273+ MSP121-specific B cells, both class-switched (IgM/Dlo) and non-class-switched (IgM/Dhi), were readily detected above background levels at 28-35dpi in P. chabaudi-infected NIMP23→Rag2-/- mixed BM chimeras (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: After resolution of infection (155-170dpi), the numbers of CD80+CD273+ and CD80+CD273— MSP121-specific B cells were either sustained or increased, while the CD80—CD273+ population decreased.
source: After resolution of infection (155-170dpi), the numbers of CD80+CD273+ and CD80+CD273— MSP121-specific B cells were either sustained or increased, while the CD80—CD273+ population decreased, compared with 28-35dpi (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: All three MSP121-specific Bmem subsets showed high CD38 expression.
source: All three MSP121-specific Bmem subsets showed high CD38 expression (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: MSP121-specific GC B cells detected at 28-35dpi did not express either CD80 or CD273.
source: Importantly, the MSP121-specific GC B cells detected at 28-35dpi did not express either CD80 or CD273, further distinguishing GC from memory and atypical memory P. chabaudi-specific B-cell subsets (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: No MSP121-specific GC B cells were detected above background level after resolution of the infection.
source: No MSP121-specific GC B cells were detected above background level after resolution of the infection (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Approximately 70% of MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ AMB observed at days 28-35pi expressed either CD80, CD273 or a combination of both.
source: Finally, and in accordance with Figure 3, approximately 70% of the MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ AMB observed at days 28-35pi expressed either CD80, CD273 or a combination of both (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: After resolution of infection (155-170dpi), MSP121-specific B cells expressing different combinations of CD80 and CD273 all expressed very high levels of FCRL5.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that after resolution of infection (155-170dpi), MSP121-specific B cells expressing different combinations of CD80 and CD273 (CD80+CD273+, CD80-CD273+ or CD80+CD273-) all expressed very high levels of FCRL5, in contrast to CD80-CD273- MSP121-specific B cells that express no memory markers at this stage (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: FCRL5 might be a marker for all Bmem.
source: This suggests that FCRL5 might be a marker for all Bmem.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all memory B cell subsets express high FCRL5.

claim: PhenoGraph analysis identified six clusters of MSP121-specific B cells with memory characteristics displaying high expression of CD38, CD80 and/or CD273, and variable expression of IgD, all of which expressed high levels of FCRL5.
source: The analysis identified six clusters of cells with memory characteristics displaying high expression of CD38, CD80 and/or CD273, and variable expression of IgD, all of which expressed high levels of FCRL5 (Figure 6C: clusters identified with purple arrows).
evidence: Supported by PhenoGraph analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MSP121-specific FCRL5hi B cells showed high expression of hallmark memory B cell markers Cd38, Cd80, Cd86, Nt5e and Pdcd1lg2.
source: As expected, the MSP121-specific FCRL5hi B cell subset showed high expression of genes encoding the hallmark memory B cell markers Cd38, Cd80, Cd86, Nt5e (CD73) and Pdcd1lg2 (CD273), when compared with either MSP121-specific FCRL5— B cells sorted at the same time or MSP121-specific B cells sorted from naïve mice (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: MSP121-specific FCRL5hi B cells sorted after resolution of infection upregulated the anti-apoptotic Bcl2 gene.
source: Moreover, the MSP121-specific FCRL5hi B cells sorted after resolution of the infection upregulated the anti-apoptotic Bcl2 gene, which is an additional hallmark characteristic of memory B cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: FCRL5 identified CD80+ and CD273+ MSP121-specific Bmem subsets generated following immunization with a model antigen.
source: Importantly, FCRL5 also identified CD80+ and CD273+ MSP121-specific Bmem subsets generated following immunization with a model antigen (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Principal component analysis demonstrated a strikingly distinct transcriptome of MSP121-specific AMB from that of MSP121-specific Bmem and all other MSP121-specific B-cell subsets.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated a strikingly distinct transcriptome of MSP121-specific AMB from that of MSP121-specific Bmem, as well as all other MSP121-specific B-cell subsets sorted in this study (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: MSP121-specific AMB and Bmem shared the expression of mouse memory markers including Cd80, Fcrl5, Nt5e, and Cd86.
source: MSP121-specific AMB sorted during chronic P. chabaudi infection, and MSP121-specific Bmem sorted after resolution of the infection shared the expression of a series of mouse memory markers, including Cd80, Fcrl5, Nt5e (CD73), and Cd86 (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: MSP121-specific Bmem showed the highest levels of expression of the anti-apoptotic Bcl2 gene, while MSP121-specific AMB showed the lowest levels.
source: While MSP121-specific Bmem from after infection resolution showed the highest levels of expression of the anti-apoptotic Bcl2 gene, MSP121-specific AMB sorted during chronic P. chabaudi infection showed the lowest levels of expression of this hallmark anti-apoptotic gene (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: MSP121-specific AMB expressed high levels of pro-apoptotic genes Bad, Bax, Fas and Fasl.
source: In contrast to MSP121-specific Bmem, MSP121-specific AMB expressed high levels of the pro-apoptotic genes Bad, Bax, Fas and Fasl (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: MSP121-specific AMB expressed very high levels of class-switched immunoglobulins, including Igha, Ighg1, Ighg2b, Ighg2c and Ighg3.
source: Interestingly, MSP121-specific AMB expressed very high levels of class-switched immunoglobulins, including Igha, Ighg1, Ighg2b, Ighg2c and Ighg3 (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: MSP121-specific AMB highly expressed Cd11b, Cd11c, Tbx21, Ifng and Pdcd1, all hallmarks of human AMB.
source: Finally, MSP121-specific AMB highly expressed Cd11b, Cd11c, Tbx21, Ifng and Pdcd1 (Figure 7E), all hallmarks of human AMB
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The increased expression of Mki67, pro-apoptotic genes and class-switched immunoglobulins in AMB suggests that they resemble activated B cells.
source: The increased expression of Mki67, pro-apoptotic genes and class-switched immunoglobulins in AMB suggests that they resemble activated B cells.
evidence: Inferred from the gene expression patterns observed in AMB.

claim: Bmem express much less Mki67 (similar to naïve cells) and present an anti-apoptotic gene expression pattern, consistent with being long-lived quiescent B cells.
source: By contrast, Bmem express much less Mki67 (similar to naïve cells) and present an anti-apoptotic gene expression pattern, consistent with being long-lived quiescent B cells.
evidence: Inferred from the gene expression patterns observed in Bmem.

claim: Mouse FCRL5 has been shown to be expressed on marginal zone and B1 B cells.
source: Mouse FCRL5 has been shown to be expressed on marginal zone (MZ) and B1 B cells (Won et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Won et al., 2006.

claim: MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ AMB are not MZ or B1 B cells based on canonical marker expression.
source: Studying all these canonical markers, we found no other similarities between B1/MZ and MSP121-specific CD11b+CD11c+ AMB to suggest a relationship between these subsets (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: Unlike MZ and B1 B cells, MSP121-specific AMB were class-switched and expressed very high levels of IgG.
source: Moreover, unlike MZ and B1 B cells, MSP121-specific AMB were class-switched and expressed very high levels of IgG (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: MSP121-specific AMB did not display a GC phenotype (CD38hiGL-7lo).
source: Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that MSP121-specific AMB did not display a GC phenotype (i.e. CD38hiGL-7lo) (Figure 8C)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: MSP121-specific CD38loGL-7hi GC B cells showed low expression of both CD11b and CD11c.
source: while the MSP121-specific CD38loGL-7hi GC B cells showed low expression of both CD11b and CD11c.
evidence: Inferred from flow cytometry data showing GC cells are distinct from AMB.

claim: P. chabaudi-specific AMB represent a distinct subset of short-lived activated B cells.
source: All together, these data further show that P. chabaudi-specific AMB represent a distinct subset of short-lived activated B cells.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing AMB are distinct from other B cell subsets and are short-lived.

claim: Reduction of HIV plasma viremia by ART resulted in a significant reduction of HIV-specific AMB without altering the frequency of HIV-specific Bmem.
source: reduction of HIV plasma viremia by ART resulted in a significant reduction of HIV-specific AMB without altering the frequency of HIV-specific Bmem (de Bree et al., 2017; Kardava et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to de Bree et al., 2017 and Kardava et al., 2014.

claim: Individuals living in high malaria endemicity present higher frequencies of AMB than individuals living in areas with moderate transmission.
source: individuals living in high malaria endemicity present higher frequencies of AMB than individuals living in areas with moderate transmission (Illingworth et al., 2013; Sullivan et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Illingworth et al., 2013 and Sullivan et al., 2015.

claim: Repetitive Plasmodium episodes result in higher frequencies of AMB.
source: repetitive Plasmodium episodes result in higher frequencies of AMB (Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017.

claim: The percentage of AMB is larger in children with persistent asymptomatic Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia as compared with parasite-free children.
source: the percentage of AMB is larger in children with persistent asymptomatic Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia as compared with parasite-free children (Weiss et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2009.

claim: Previously exposed subjects significantly reduce the frequency of AMB following a year of continuous absence of exposure to Plasmodium falciparum infection.
source: previously exposed subjects significantly reduce the frequency of AMB following a year of continuous absence of exposure to Plasmodium falciparum infection (Ayieko et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ayieko et al., 2013.

claim: Constant immune activation rather than impaired memory function leads to the accumulation of AMB in malaria.
source: These observations all support the view that constant immune activation rather than impaired memory function leads to the accumulation of AMB in malaria.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that AMB frequency correlates with ongoing infection and decreases with infection resolution.

claim: P. chabaudi-specific Bmem included both class-switched and non-class-switched cells, which show different responses to a secondary challenge infection.
source: P. chabaudi-specific Bmem included both class-switched and non-class-switched cells, which show different responses to a secondary challenge infection (Krishnamurty et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krishnamurty et al., 2016.

claim: The expansion of AMB in malaria is not a consequence of B-cell exhaustion, but rather a physiologic stage of B-cell activation.
source: Our data suggest that the expansion of AMB in malaria is not a consequence of B-cell exhaustion, but rather a physiologic stage of B-cell activation, and that these cells are sustained in high frequencies by ongoing chronic infections.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing AMB are short-lived, activated cells that disappear after infection resolution.

claim: Plasmodium-specific AMB are sustained in high frequencies by ongoing chronic infections.
source: Our data suggest that the expansion of AMB in malaria is not a consequence of B-cell exhaustion, but rather a physiologic stage of B-cell activation, and that these cells are sustained in high frequencies by ongoing chronic infections.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing AMB disappear after infection resolution.

claim: Robust expansion of Plasmodium-specific AMB does not hinder clearance of the infection, activation of germinal centers, or generation of Plasmodium-specific long-lived quiescent Bmem upon resolution of the infection.
source: Importantly, our data demonstrate that robust expansion of Plasmodium-specific AMB does not hinder clearance of the infection, activation of germinal centers, or generation of Plasmodium-specific long-lived quiescent Bmem upon resolution of the infection.
evidence: Supported by data showing infection is cleared, GC are formed, and Bmem persist after infection resolution despite AMB expansion.

claim: T-bet+ atypical B cells are critical to eradicate various murine viral infections.
source: T-bet+ atypical B cells are critical to eradicate various murine viral infections (Barnett et al., 2016; Rubtsova et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Barnett et al., 2016 and Rubtsova et al., 2013.

claim: Yellow fever and vaccinia vaccinations of humans stimulated an acute T-bet+ B-cell response.
source: and a recent study showed that yellow fever and vaccinia vaccinations of humans stimulated an acute T-bet+ B-cell response and suggested that these T-bet+ B-cell population may function as an early responder during acute viral infections (Knox et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knox et al., 2017a.

claim: Expansion of AMB associated with malaria is driven by IFNγ.
source: Moreover, similar to ABC, expansion of human AMB associated with malaria is driven by IFNγ (Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Obeng-Adjei et al., 2017.

claim: IL-21 directly promotes T-bet expression in B cells in the context of TLR engagement.
source: IL-21, which is highly expressed by follicular helper T cells in response to Plasmodium infection (Carpio et al., 2015; Obeng-Adjei et al., 2015; Pérez-Mazliah et al., 2015), also directly promotes T-bet expression in B cells in the context of TLR engagement (Naradikian et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carpio et al., 2015; Obeng-Adjei et al., 2015; Pérez-Mazliah et al., 2015; Naradikian et al., 2016b.

claim: BCRs cloned from P. falciparum-specific AMB from malaria-exposed adults encode P. falciparum-specific IgG antibodies, which could contribute to P. falciparum-specific IgG antibodies in serum.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that BCRs cloned from P. falciparum-specific AMB from malaria-exposed adults encode P. falciparum-specific IgG antibodies, which could contribute to P. falciparum-specific IgG antibodies in serum (Muellenbeck et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muellenbeck et al., 2013.

claim: P. falciparum-specific AMB do not prevent, but rather contribute to the control of Plasmodium infection.
source: These authors proposed that P. falciparum-specific AMB do not prevent, but rather contribute to the control of Plasmodium infection.
evidence: This is a statement about what other authors proposed, supported by citation to Muellenbeck et al., 2013.

claim: Generation of Plasmodium-specific AMB does not prevent the generation of Plasmodium-specific Bmem.
source: Moreover, we show that generation of Plasmodium-specific AMB does not prevent the generation of Plasmodium-specific Bmem, and does not prevent resolution of the infection.
evidence: Supported by data showing both AMB and Bmem are present during infection, and Bmem persist after resolution.

claim: Generation of Plasmodium-specific AMB does not prevent resolution of the infection.
source: Moreover, we show that generation of Plasmodium-specific AMB does not prevent the generation of Plasmodium-specific Bmem, and does not prevent resolution of the infection.
evidence: Supported by data showing infection is resolved despite AMB generation.

claim: In this chronic P. chabaudi infection, AMB require ongoing antigenic stimulation driven by the sub-patent infection to persist.
source: In this chronic P. chabaudi infection, it appears that AMB require ongoing antigenic stimulation driven by the sub-patent infection to persist, and do not represent a true long-lived 'memory' B cell subset.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AMB disappear after infection resolution.

claim: AMB do not represent a true long-lived 'memory' B cell subset.
source: In this chronic P. chabaudi infection, it appears that AMB require ongoing antigenic stimulation driven by the sub-patent infection to persist, and do not represent a true long-lived 'memory' B cell subset.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing AMB are short-lived and disappear after infection resolution.

claim: The IghNIMP23/+ mice were healthy with no unusual behavioral or physical characteristics.
source: The IghNIMP23/+ mice were healthy, with no unusual behavioral or physical characteristics.
evidence: This is an observation from the mouse model generation.

claim: There were no alterations in B cell populations in the bone marrow of IghNIMP23/+ mice compared to wild-type littermates.
source: There were no alterations in total cellularity, pro-B, pre-B, immature B, mature B, total B220+CD19+ B cells, and plasma cells in the bone marrow (Figure 1A–B)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: There were no alterations in B cell populations in the spleen of IghNIMP23/+ mice compared to wild-type littermates.
source: and no alterations in number of T1, T2, T3, follicular, marginal zone, germinal center B cells, plasmablasts, plasma cells, and total cellularity in the spleen of IghNIMP23/+ mice (Figure 1C–D)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Infection of C57BL/6J wt mice with P. chabaudi by mosquito bite gives rise to a short (48 hr) pre-erythrocytic infection, followed by an acute blood parasitemia peaking approximately 10d post-transmission.
source: Infection of C57BL/6J wt mice with P. chabaudi by mosquito bite gives rise to a short (48 hr) pre-erythrocytic infection, followed by an acute blood parasitemia peaking approximately 10d post-transmission. Thereafter, the infection is rapidly controlled, reaching very low parasitemias by 15d post-transmission, with a subsequent prolonged (~90 d), but low-level chronic infection before parasite elimination (Brugat et al., 2017; Spence et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brugat et al., 2017 and Spence et al., 2013.

claim: P. chabaudi infection is rapidly controlled, reaching very low parasitemias by 15d post-transmission, with a subsequent prolonged (~90 d), but low-level chronic infection before parasite elimination.
source: Thereafter, the infection is rapidly controlled, reaching very low parasitemias by 15d post-transmission, with a subsequent prolonged (~90 d), but low-level chronic infection before parasite elimination (Brugat et al., 2017; Spence et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brugat et al., 2017 and Spence et al., 2013.

claim: Mouse FCRL5 most closely resembles human FCRL3.
source: Mouse FCRL5 most closely resembles human FCRL3 and is the only mouse FCRL-family member which contains both ITIM and ITAM motifs in its cytoplasmic tail (Davis, 2007; Davis et al., 2004; Won et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davis, 2007; Davis et al., 2004; Won et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2013.

claim: Mouse FCRL5 is the only mouse FCRL-family member which contains both ITIM and ITAM motifs in its cytoplasmic tail.
source: Mouse FCRL5 most closely resembles human FCRL3 and is the only mouse FCRL-family member which contains both ITIM and ITAM motifs in its cytoplasmic tail (Davis, 2007; Davis et al., 2004; Won et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davis, 2007; Davis et al., 2004; Won et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2013.

claim: CD80 and CD273 identify mouse B cells that are antigen-experienced and potentially memory cells.
source: Therefore, our flow cytometry panel for mouse AMB included antibodies against CD11b, CD11c, FCRL5, CD21, IgD, and also CD80 and CD273 which identify mouse B cells that are antigen-experienced and potentially memory cells (Anderson et al., 2007; Tomayko et al., 2010; Zuccarino-Catania et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2007; Tomayko et al., 2010; Zuccarino-Catania et al., 2014.

claim: CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific mouse AMB present during the chronic phase of P. chabaudi infection are very similar to human AMB described in several chronic infections.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific mouse AMB present during the chronic phase of P. chabaudi infection are very similar to human AMB described in several chronic infections.
evidence: Inferred from the transcriptome analysis showing similar gene expression patterns.

claim: CD11b+CD11c+ MSP121-specific B cells show features of activation, proliferation, DNA replication and plasmablasts, resembling previous observations in human AMB.
source: In addition, this B-cell subset shows features of activation, proliferation, DNA replication and plasmablasts, resembling previous observations in human AMB (Muellenbeck et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data and citation to Muellenbeck et al., 2013.
